title: Read the sky: clouds as a six-hour forecast
description: Every cloud shows you something the air is doing. Work out what an anvil, a lens over a ridge, a ring around the sun, or a row of hanging pouches tells you about the next few hours. Each question starts with a photograph, and each answer comes with a diagram of the mechanism.
author: Quizbun

questions.title: Thin hooked streaks spread across the sky through the morning and slowly thicken. What do the next six hours look like?

images.alt: A blue sky filled with thin white cirrus streaks. Each has a small dense tuft at one end and a long fibrous tail trailing away from it, giving them a hooked, comma-like shape.
images.caption: Cirrus uncinus, the shape that earned the folk name mare's tails. Photo by ADARSHluck, CC BY-SA 4.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cirrus_uncinus_clouds_in_the_morning_sky.jpg).

images.alt: A cross-section through an approaching warm front. Warm air slides up a shallow wedge of cold air, and the cloud deck thickens and lowers from thin cirrus at the leading edge through cirrostratus and altostratus to nimbostratus and steady rain at the front itself. Time labels along the ground show the rain arriving about twenty hours after the cirrus.

options.text: Dry. These are ice clouds far too high to rain on you, and the weather they announce is still most of a day away
Rain within the hour, because these streaks are the leading edge of a rain band
Thunderstorms by early afternoon, because the hooks show strong vertical motion
Impossible to say. High clouds form and clear at random and carry no information about what follows

questions.explanation:
Cirrus sits between roughly 6 and 12 km up and is made entirely of ice, so nothing it drops survives the fall to the ground. The hook is a small head where the crystals form. Heavier crystals fall out of that head, and wind that changes speed with height sweeps them into the long tail.

A single glance at cirrus says little, so watch how it changes. Cirrus that arrives from one direction, spreads, and thickens is the top of a wedge of warm air climbing over colder air ahead of it. That wedge is shallow, sloping something like 1 in 150, so the surface front and its rain trail 600 to 1000 km behind the first cirrus. At a typical 40 km/h, that is 15 to 25 hours. Six hours from now the sky will probably have gone milky. The rain is for tomorrow.

questions.title: A pale ring circles the sun about an outstretched hand-span away from it. What does the ring prove about the cloud you are looking through?

images.alt: A bright whitish sky with a large circular halo around the sun, which is hidden behind the dark silhouette of a tree. Faint fibrous cirrostratus texture is visible across the sky inside and outside the ring.
images.caption: A 22° halo in cirrostratus fibratus. Photo by Eduardo Marquetti, CC BY-SA 2.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cirrostratus_fibratus_with_22_degrees_halo.jpg).

images.alt: A ray of sunlight enters one side face of a hexagonal ice crystal and leaves through a face sixty degrees around, bending twice. The angle between the original direction and the exit ray is marked as 22 degrees. A second panel shows the sun with a dashed ring drawn 22 degrees out from it.

options.text: The veil is made of hexagonal ice crystals
The veil is made of water droplets that happen to be very uniform in size
The air between you and the sun is carrying an unusual amount of dust
The cloud is low enough that you are seeing it through haze near the ground

questions.explanation:
Only hexagonal ice can draw this ring. A hexagonal prism refracts sunlight twice, once where the ray enters a side face and once where it leaves through a face 60° around. How far it bends depends on how the crystal happens to be turned, but there is a floor. With a refractive index near 1.31, no orientation of an ice prism bends the ray less than about 21.8°. Rays pile up at that minimum and thin out beyond it, so a bright ring appears 22° from the sun, and the sky just inside the ring looks darker than the sky outside it.

Water droplets cannot do this. They make a corona instead, a much smaller coloured disc pressed close around the sun, and its width varies with droplet size.

So a halo means a thin veil of ice, which in practice usually means cirrostratus, the second stage of the warm-front sequence. That is why the old rhyme about a ring around the moon bringing rain does better than chance. The lead time is still 12 to 24 hours.

questions.title: The sun has gone from a sharp disc to a pale smear behind a grey sheet, and your shadow has disappeared. How far along is the front?

images.alt: A featureless grey sky covering the whole frame, with the sun showing through as a diffuse pale blur with no sharp edge. A few darker cloud fragments drift below the main sheet.
images.caption: Altostratus translucidus. The sun is still up there, but the edge of the disc has gone. Photo by Couch-scratching-cats, public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Altostratus_translucidus_1.jpg).

images.alt: Three panels showing the same front at three stages. Under cirrostratus the sun is a sharp disc with a halo and a post casts a crisp shadow. Under altostratus the sun is a pale watery blur and the shadow has gone. Under nimbostratus the sun is invisible and steady rain is falling.

options.text: Close. Once shadows go, rain usually starts within a few hours
Barely started. This stage typically runs for two or three days before any rain
Already past. The sun dims like this as a front moves away from you
No way to tell. This look happens at any point in any weather system

questions.explanation:
Altostratus sits between about 2 and 6 km and holds a mix of water droplets and ice crystals. It runs from a few hundred metres to a couple of kilometres thick, and that thickness is what you read when you look at the sun.

Your shadow disappears once the deck blocks enough direct sunlight, so the layer overhead has already thickened a long way from the thin ice veil that made the halo. Next in the sequence is nimbostratus, which is lower, hides the sun completely, and gives the rain.

Altostratus often drops virga that evaporates before it lands, so a first sprinkle that never becomes proper rain fits the same picture.

questions.title: Cirrus came through last night, a halo appeared this morning, and now the sun is a watery blur. The deck keeps lowering and thickening. Name the cloud it becomes when the rain starts.
questions.description: One word, the Latin genus name.

images.alt: A height scale from the ground to twelve kilometres. Cirrus sits near ten kilometres and cirrostratus near seven, both made of ice. Altostratus fills the middle levels between three and five kilometres. Nimbostratus sits below two and a half kilometres with rain falling from its base.

questions.explanation:
The sequence runs cirrus, cirrostratus, altostratus, nimbostratus, each one lower and thicker than the last. Nimbostratus sits below about 2 km, hides the sun completely, and gives long steady rain rather than showers. The *nimbo-* part of the name means rain.

The heights explain the order. A warm front is a shallow ramp, so its highest, thinnest cloud reaches you first and its lowest, thickest cloud last. Seeing the sequence run backwards, a grey sheet breaking up into mid-level cloud and then into high wisps, means the front has passed.

questions.title: Yesterday the contrails vanished a few plane-lengths behind the aircraft. Today they hang around for hours and spread into broad fuzzy bands. What changed?

images.alt: A blue sky crossed by three aircraft contrails. One is thin and sharply defined. The other two have broadened into wide soft-edged bands with ragged structure, several times the width of the fresh one.
images.caption: One fresh trail and two older ones that have spread. What separates them is age. Photo by Iamdev37, CC BY-SA 4.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Three_Contrails_(Condensation_Trail)_visible_simultaneously.jpg).

images.alt: Two panels. In dry air the contrail is a short stub behind the aircraft that evaporates within seconds. In air that already holds more water vapour than ice can tolerate, the trail widens with age into a broad band that is still there an hour later.

options.text: The air at cruise height is now humid enough that the ice crystals grow instead of evaporating
The aircraft are burning a different fuel blend
The aircraft are flying lower today, through warmer air
The wind aloft has dropped, so the trails are no longer being torn apart

questions.explanation:
Every contrail starts the same way: water vapour in the exhaust condenses and freezes onto soot particles within a wingspan or two of the engines. What happens after that depends on the air the aircraft is flying through.

If that air holds less water vapour than ice can tolerate, the crystals lose molecules faster than they gain them and the line is gone in seconds. If the air is supersaturated with respect to ice, the crystals gain molecules instead. They grow, fall a little, the wind shears them sideways, and the trail widens with age. Some spread into sheets you can barely tell from natural cirrus.

A contrail is therefore a free humidity reading for a layer you cannot otherwise sample. Ice supersaturation at cruise height often goes with moist air running ahead of a warm front, so persistent spreading trails are a rough hint that the pattern is changing.

questions.title: Small puffy clouds dot the sky, each wider than it is tall, and every one has its flat bottom at the same height. Why do the bottoms line up?

images.alt: A deep blue sky over dry grassland, scattered with many small white cumulus clouds. Each is wider than it is tall, and their flat grey bases all sit at one common level across the whole sky.
images.caption: Cumulus humilis over a paddock. Note how the bases form a single horizontal line across the frame. Photo by Toby Hudson, CC BY-SA 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cumulus_humilis_clouds.jpg).

images.alt: Warm bubbles rise from a bare field, a car park, and a sunny hillside. Each cools at the same rate as it climbs and reaches its dew point at the same altitude, so condensation starts at one shared level and every cloud is cut off with a flat bottom there.

options.text: Each cloud starts where its rising air cools to the dew point, and that happens at the same height across the whole area
They are resting on a layer of denser air below them that acts like a floor
They all formed at the same moment and have since settled to a common level
It is an optical effect. The bases really are at different heights but look level from below

questions.explanation:
A bubble of air leaving a warm patch of ground is unsaturated, so as it rises and expands it cools at close to 9.8 °C per kilometre. Its dew point falls too, but only about 1.8 °C per kilometre, because the parcel spreads its water vapour through a growing volume. The two values close on each other and meet at one height, and condensation begins there. Meteorologists call it the lifting condensation level.

Air over a field, a car park and a hillside starts at slightly different temperatures but shares roughly the same temperature and humidity profile, so every bubble saturates at the same altitude. The flat bottom is a line drawn by temperature, and nothing is holding the cloud up.

Cumulus humilis, wider than tall with tops that have stopped growing, means shallow convection under a stable layer. The next few hours are fine, and the clouds usually dissolve as the ground cools towards evening.

questions.title: The air is 27 °C and the dew point is 15 °C. Roughly how high is the base of the cumulus forming overhead, in metres?
questions.description: Use the rule of thumb that the gap between temperature and dew point closes at about 8 °C for every kilometre of climb.

images.alt: A plot of temperature and dew point against height. The temperature line falls about ten degrees Celsius per kilometre and the dew point line about two, so the twelve-degree gap at the surface closes and the two lines meet at roughly 1.5 kilometres, which is cloud base.

questions.explanation:
The spread is 27 − 15 = 12 °C. At 8 °C per kilometre that closes after 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5 km, so cloud base is around 1500 m.

The 8 is the difference between two rates. Rising unsaturated air cools at about 9.8 °C per kilometre while its dew point drops at about 1.8 °C per kilometre, leaving roughly 8 °C per kilometre of closing. Turned around, that is about 125 m of climb per degree of surface spread. Pilots do the same sum in feet with a factor of 400, which gives 4800 ft here, near enough the same answer.

The estimate assumes a parcel that rises without mixing with the air around it. Real bubbles pull in drier air on the way up, so measured bases often come out a little higher than the rule predicts, especially on dry, windy days.

questions.title: A tower has grown fast all afternoon and its top is still a crisp, hard-edged cauliflower. What does that sharpness tell you?

images.alt: A tall white cloud tower against blue sky, built of tightly packed rounded lumps. Its edges are sharply defined against the sky, with no wispy or fibrous texture anywhere on the top.
images.caption: Cumulus congestus. Every lump on that top has a hard edge. Photo by Bidgee, CC BY-SA 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cumulus_congestus_cloud.jpg).

images.alt: Two towers compared. The first has a crisp cauliflower outline because it is still made of liquid droplets and produces no lightning. The second has frozen at the top, which blurs its outline into fibrous strands and lets colliding ice particles separate charge, so it can produce lightning.

options.text: The top is still liquid water, so the cloud cannot be producing lightning yet
The cloud has stopped growing and will start to flatten out within minutes
The cloud is too shallow to produce rain of any kind
The cloud is rotating, which is what keeps its edges so well defined

questions.explanation:
The outline tells you which phase the cloud top is in. A top made of liquid droplets keeps a hard edge, because droplets that stray into the dry air outside evaporate almost at once and the boundary stays sharp. Once the top freezes into ice crystals, that edge softens into fibrous strands that trail away, and the cloud is now a cumulonimbus.

Freezing also decides the lightning. Charge separation depends on collisions between soft hail and small ice crystals with supercooled water present, so a storm can electrify only once its upper part has frozen.

A congestus this size will usually give a shower within an hour or two. Whether it becomes a storm depends on whether it keeps climbing past the freezing level, and the top is where you watch for the answer.

questions.title: The storm's top has stopped climbing and spread sideways into a flat sheet. What stopped it?

images.alt: A large cumulonimbus cloud over a city skyline at sunset. Its lower part is a tall lumpy tower, and its top spreads abruptly outward into a broad flat-topped sheet that overhangs the tower on one side.
images.caption: Cumulonimbus incus over Warsaw. Everything below the flat top is still rising; everything at the top has nowhere left to go. Photo by Kamil Nowacki, CC BY-SA 4.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cumulonimbus_incus_over_Warsaw,_Poland.jpg).

images.alt: A storm updraft rises until it reaches the tropopause, marked as the level above which the air stops getting colder with height. The rising air loses its buoyancy there, has nowhere left to go, and spreads sideways, drawn downwind by strong winds at that level into a long flat anvil.

options.text: It reached the tropopause, where the air above is no longer colder, so the rising air ran out of buoyancy
It ran out of moisture, and a cloud cannot grow any further without more water
It reached the height where water vapour freezes, which acts as a hard ceiling
It hit the jet stream, whose horizontal speed shears off any cloud that reaches it

questions.explanation:
An updraft keeps rising for as long as it is warmer, and therefore less dense, than the air around it. Through the troposphere the temperature drops with height, so a rising parcel can stay ahead of its surroundings. At the tropopause that stops. Above it the temperature holds steady and then increases, so a parcel pushed any higher is immediately colder than its surroundings and sinks back.

With nowhere left to climb, the air spreads sideways, and the strong winds at that level stretch it downwind into the anvil. The overhang then points the way the storm is travelling. A lump poking up through the otherwise flat top, an overshooting top, marks an updraft strong enough to punch briefly into the stratosphere, which goes with the more severe storms.

questions.title: Rounded pouches hang from the underside of a storm's anvil. What is the air inside those pouches doing?

images.alt: A dark cloud layer covering the sky above a range of hills, with dozens of smooth rounded pouches hanging down from its underside like a field of inverted bubbles.
images.caption: Mammatus over Montana. Every lobe bulges downward, the opposite of a cumulus top. Photo by Acroterion, CC BY-SA 4.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Mammatus_clouds_Montana_MT1.jpg).

images.alt: Two panels. Ordinary cumulus bubbles push upward and their tops bulge up. Mammatus are the reverse: pockets of cloudy ice-laden air sink out of the underside of an anvil into drier air below, where evaporation chills them and keeps them sinking.

options.text: Sinking. Cloudy air is dropping into drier air below and chilling itself as its ice and water evaporate
Rising, in the same way that the bubbles on top of a cumulus rise
Rotating about horizontal axes, which is why tornadoes so often follow
Holding still while the clear air around it rises past

questions.explanation:
Mammatus run convection backwards. Ice-laden air from the anvil sinks into the drier air underneath. As that ice sublimates and any droplets evaporate, the pocket loses heat, becomes denser than its surroundings, and keeps sinking, which is what holds the lobes together instead of letting them mix away.

Two bits of folklore need correcting. Mammatus form under the spreading anvil, and the anvil lies downwind of the storm's core, so you usually see them as a storm passes or after it has gone, not before it arrives. And although they turn up with severe storms, they say nothing about tornadoes. A tornado forms in the rotating updraft at the inflow end of a supercell, the opposite end from the anvil you are standing under.

questions.title: A low, layered wedge stretches across the horizon under an approaching storm, with brighter sky underneath it. What arrives first, and how soon?

images.alt: A dark low cloud wedge stretching right across the horizon beneath a line of taller clouds, its underside ragged and layered, with a bright strip of open sky visible below and behind it.
images.caption: A gust collar running ahead of a storm line in Kansas. The bright strip underneath is air the rain has not reached yet. Photo by GerritR, CC BY-SA 4.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Linienf%C3%B6rmig_angeordneter_Cumulus_mit_B%C3%B6enkragen_in_Kansas_II.jpg).

images.alt: Rain-cooled air falls out of a storm, spreads along the ground as a dense pool, and runs out ahead of the rain. Warm humid air is forced up over the nose of that pool and condenses into the wedge-shaped shelf cloud, so the gust arrives at the nose and the rain follows minutes later.

options.text: A sharp burst of wind, within minutes, with the rain a few minutes behind it
Rain first, building gradually over the next half hour
Hail first, because the wedge is the part of the storm where hail falls out
Nothing. The wedge marks the back edge of a storm that has already gone past

questions.explanation:
Rain falling through a storm drags air down with it and chills that air by evaporation. The result is a pool of dense air sitting on the ground, and like water poured onto a table it spreads outward, running ahead of the rain that made it.

Where the leading edge of that pool undercuts the warm humid air in front of the storm, it shoves that air upward. The air cools as it rises, reaches its dew point, and condenses into the shelf cloud. You are looking at the boundary itself, lit from below by sky the storm has not covered yet.

The order follows from the geometry. The cold air reaches you first as a sudden wind shift and a gust, often the strongest wind of the whole event, and the rain catches up when the core does. A shelf cloud is attached to the storm's leading edge and looks like a wedge or a set of stacked steps. A wall cloud is a different feature: an isolated lowering under the rain-free base on the inflow side, and that one can rotate.

questions.title: A smooth lens-shaped cloud has hung in the same spot over a mountain for three hours, while the wind at that height is around 80 km/h. How does it stay put?

images.alt: A snow-covered volcanic peak at dusk with a large smooth lens-shaped cloud stacked above and beside it. The cloud has sharp, almost polished edges and a layered structure, quite unlike the ragged clouds elsewhere in the frame.
images.caption: Lenticular clouds over Mount Rainier. Photo by loggedout, CC BY 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Mt._Rainier-Lenticular_Cloud_-_panoramio.jpg).

images.alt: Stable air forced over a ridge oscillates in a standing wave downwind. Air condenses climbing into each crest and evaporates descending out of it, so cloud is made continuously at the upwind edge and destroyed at the downwind edge while the crests stay anchored to the terrain.

options.text: The air is streaming straight through it. Cloud condenses at the upwind edge and evaporates at the downwind edge, so the shape holds still while the air keeps moving
The mountain shelters a pocket of calm air behind it where the cloud can sit undisturbed
The cloud is dense enough to resist the wind and stays anchored by its own weight
It is far higher than it looks, in a layer where the wind happens to be calm

questions.explanation:
Stable air pushed up over a ridge overshoots, sinks back past its resting level, overshoots again, and keeps oscillating downwind as a standing wave. The wave is anchored to the terrain that made it, so its crests stay in one place on the map while air pours through them.

Air climbing into a crest cools, and if it passes its dew point it condenses. Descending out of the crest it warms again and the droplets evaporate. Cloud forms at the upwind face and evaporates at the downwind face at the same rate, which is how something can look this solid, keep a polished edge, and stay put for hours.

For the next six hours this is a wind forecast: strong flow aloft, turbulence, and often rough air in the lee of the range. Glider pilots climb in the smooth rising part of the wave and stay out of the rotor churning underneath it.

questions.title: At nine in the morning, small turrets and tufts are sprouting upward from a mid-level cloud layer. What does that suggest about the afternoon?

images.alt: A blue sky filled with a broad field of small white mid-level cloud elements arranged in rows. Many of them have ragged tufted tops that sprout upward from their bases rather than lying flat.
images.caption: Altocumulus castellanus and floccus. The tufts are convection happening four kilometres up. Photo by Daniele.Brundu, CC BY 4.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Altocumulus_castellanus_undulatus,_Altocumulus_floccus_and_Cirrocumulus_floccus.jpg).

images.alt: Two panels. At nine in the morning little turrets sprout from a flat mid-level layer while the ground is still cool, showing the air at four kilometres is already unstable. By three in the afternoon, surface bubbles driven by a hot ground finally reach that layer and keep climbing into a storm.

options.text: Storms are more likely than usual, because the air several kilometres up is already unstable
A settled, quiet day, because the turrets show the layer is capped and cannot grow
Rain within the hour, because the turrets are already producing it
Fog by evening, as the moisture from the layer settles towards the ground

questions.explanation:
Castellanus and floccus are the forms of altocumulus that show convection happening at cloud level rather than being driven from the ground. A turret sprouting out of a layer means the air at that height is unstable. Something nudged a parcel upward and it kept going on its own.

The hour is what makes this useful. At nine in the morning the ground has not had time to drive anything, so the rising air you see at 4 km did not come from the surface. When afternoon heating finally does lift surface bubbles that high, they arrive in a layer that lets them keep climbing instead of flattening them out.

Forecasters treat morning castellanus as one of the more reliable sky-based hints of afternoon thunderstorms, which makes it a rare case of a cloud that really does forecast six hours ahead.

questions.title: Grey streaks hang below a cloud and fade out well above the ground. What should you expect underneath them?

images.alt: A heavy grey cloud layer with dense streaks of falling precipitation trailing from its base. The streaks thin out and disappear partway down, leaving a clear bright gap between them and the dark hills below.
images.caption: Virga below nimbostratus. Rain is falling, and none of it is landing. Photo by Simon A. Eugster, CC BY-SA 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Nimbostratus_virga_grey_with_hills.jpg).

images.alt: Drops falling out of a cloud into a dry layer evaporate before reaching the ground. Evaporation takes heat from the air around them, making it denser than its surroundings, so it accelerates downward and spreads out as a gust on landing.

options.text: Dry ground, and possibly a sudden gust of wind
Light drizzle, because some fraction of the rain always makes it down
Nothing measurable, because the air below the streaks is unaffected
Fog, as the evaporated water saturates the air near the ground

questions.explanation:
Virga is precipitation that evaporates on the way down, which tells you the layer between the cloud and the ground is dry. The ground stays dry with it.

Evaporation also changes that layer. Turning water into vapour takes latent heat, and it takes it from the air the drops are falling through. That air gets colder and therefore denser than its surroundings, so it accelerates downward instead of slowing. When it reaches the surface it has to go somewhere, and it spreads out sideways.

Over deserts and high plains, where the dry layer beneath a storm can be several kilometres deep, this produces a dry microburst: a strong, sudden, rain-free gust that has caused aircraft accidents on approach. A sky that is visibly raining on nothing is worth a second look before you put up an awning or launch a small aircraft.

questions.title: Electric-blue filaments glow in a deep midsummer twilight, an hour after the sun has set. What do they tell you about tomorrow's weather?

images.alt: A dark twilight sky above a black hillside, filled with wispy pale blue cloud filaments that glow against the deep blue background while the horizon below still shows orange afterglow.
images.caption: Noctilucent clouds over Slovakia in June. The sun is below the horizon for the photographer and still shining on the cloud. Photo by Chmee2, CC BY-SA 4.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Noctilucent_clouds_over_Slovakia_in_21st_of_June,_2019_(1).jpg).

images.alt: A height scale from the ground to ninety kilometres. Every cloud that rains, shades, or gusts lives in the lowest twelve kilometres, while noctilucent clouds form near eighty kilometres with about sixty-eight kilometres of very thin air in between.

options.text: Nothing. They form around 80 km up, far above the layer where weather happens
Rain within two days, because they are the highest member of the warm-front sequence
A hard frost tonight, because they only appear when the surface air is very cold
Strong wind tomorrow, because they mark the top of the jet stream

questions.explanation:
Noctilucent clouds form near the mesopause, about 76 to 85 km up, in the coldest air on the planet. Summer polar mesospheric temperatures fall below −120 °C, cold enough for the tiny amount of water vapour up there to freeze onto dust that meteors leave behind. You see them only in deep twilight, when the sun has set for you but still lights that layer from below the horizon, and mostly between about 50° and 70° latitude from late spring to late summer.

Everything that rains, shades, or gusts on you happens in the troposphere, the lowest 8 to 15 km depending on latitude. The air at 80 km is around a hundred thousand times thinner than the air at your feet, and nothing that happens there reaches the ground as weather.

questions.title: Which of these sights mean the weather where you are standing will actually change within the next six hours?

options.text: Turrets sprouting from a mid-level layer at breakfast time
A low layered wedge racing ahead of a dark storm base
The sun fading to a watery blur behind a thickening grey sheet
Thin hooked streaks high overhead on an otherwise blue morning
Blue filaments glowing in the northern sky an hour after a June sunset

questions.explanation:
Height and sharpness set the lead time, and they mostly track each other.

High ice clouds are the earliest warning and the longest wait. Cirrus thickening in from one direction puts a warm front's rain 12 to 24 hours out, so six hours later you have a milky sky and dry shoes. Mid-level signs come due sooner. Losing your shadow behind altostratus means rain in a few hours, and morning castellanus means storms by mid-afternoon. Low, sharply defined features give the least warning of all, and a shelf cloud on the horizon leaves you minutes to get the windows shut.

Noctilucent clouds are not part of the system. At 80 km they sit several times higher than the top of the tallest thunderstorm, in air far too thin to carry weather down to you.
